4.7.name: 4.07.md
4.7.text:
An overflow occurs when an object is assigned a value that is outside the range of values that its type can represents, in which case the value of the object "wraps around" when it reaches its type limits. (p. 140) Since the resulting value after the "wrap around" is implementation dependent, an overflow is an undefined behaviour.

The followings are examples of type overflow tested on my machine.

#include <limits>

int a = std::numeric_limits<int>::max() + 1; // -2147483648 int a = std::numeric_limits<int>::min() - 1; // 2147483647 unsigned ua = 4294967295 + 5; // 4

4.8.name: 4.08.md
4.8.text:
With Logical AND and logical OR operators the operands are evaluated from left to right. Moreover, the right operand is evaluated only if the result cannot be determined by the left operand. This is known as short-circuit evaluation.

The operands of equality operators are also evaluated from left to right; however, unlike the case in the AND and OR operators, both operands must be evaluated in order to determine the result.

4.9.name: 4.09.md
4.9.text:
```cpp
const char *cp = "Hello World";
if (cp && *cp)
```

The if statement evaluates if the value of the pointer cp is not zero AND that the value it points to is not the null character '\0'. The former test checks whether or not cp is a valid pointer (points to a valid memory address), while the latter checks if cp points to the end of a c-style string (or to an empty string).

Both tests will pass: cp is valid because it points to a const char *, and that the value of the object it points to is the beginning address of the string literal, which is the character 'H'.

The if statement uses the short-circuit evaluation technique to make sure not to dereference an invalid pointer--as it is an error to do so--before checking the value cp points to.

Other verbose ways of writing this if statement:

```cpp
if (cp != 0 && *cp != '\0')
	/* ... */
```

```text
OR
```

```cpp
if (cp != NULL && *cp != '\0')
	/* ... */
```

```text
OR
```

```cpp
if (cp != nullptr && *cp != '\0') // preferred
	/* ... */
```

4.12.text: The operator < has a higher precedence than !=. Accordingly, j < k is evaluated first, which would result in either 0 or 1 (true or false). Thus, the entire expression i != j < k means that i must not equal the result of j < k. In other words, the result of expressions on either side of the operator != must not equal each other.

4.14.text:
```cpp
if (42 = i) // ...
if (i = 42) // ...
```

if (42 = i) // ERROR: 42 is an rvalue, which is not assignable. The code

```text
			will not compile.
```

if (i = 42) // BUG: i is assigned the value of 42. The result of the

```text
			statement is always true. Most certainly the intention
			was i == 42.
```

Note: writing the condition expression as

```cpp
if (42 == i) // ...
```

is a trick to guard against the aforementioned bug: if the condition were mistakenly written as 42 = i, the code will not compile. This strategy, however, will not work when comparing two lvalues, e.g.: a = b or b = a will compile fine as a condition statement.

4.17.name: 4.17.md
4.17.text: The prefix increment adds 1 to the operand and then yields the change as a result, while the postfix yields its operand and then adds 1 to it. In other words, the former returns a changed value as a result, while the latter returns a copy of the original, "unchanged value as a result". (p.148) Both require an lvalue operands. The prefix returns an lvalue and the postfix an rvalue. The prefix and postfix decrement operators work the same way.

4.24.name: 4.24.md
4.24.text:
Since we are nesting conditional operations, we are essentially grouping expressions with each others using operators of equal precedence, i.e., two ?: operators. Here, the rules of associativity dictates how the expressions of these operators are grouped together and eventually evaluated. Right associativity means that they will be grouped from right to left as such:

```cpp
finalgrade = (grade > 90) ? "high pass" : ((grade < 60) ? "fail" : "pass");
```

Note how this grouping means that outer conditional operation will not be evaluated until the inner one is evaluated first, if the grade is less than or equal to 90.

If the operator were left associative we would have the following grouping instead:

```cpp
finalgrade = ((grade > 90) ? "high pass" : (grade < 60)) ? "fail" : "pass";
```

This would result in a compile error because the outer conditional operator would have incompatible operand types: const char * and bool.

4.25.name: 4.25.md
4.25.text:
In the expression ~'q' << 6, after the bitwise NOT is evaluated the bitwise left-shift operator will perform an implicit conversion, whereby the result of ~'q' is promoted to a signed int (since 6 is of type signed int). (p. 152, 160)

```text
~'q' returns 0x8e
```

```cpp
0xffffff8e << 6; // converted to a signed int
```

Given that shifting a signed number is implementation dependent the expression invokes undefined behaviour. (p. 153)

That said, on this machine the result is

```text
0xffffe380 or 1111 1111 1111 1111 1110 0011 1000 0000
```

4.26.name: 4.26.md
4.26.text: Using an unsigned int instead of an unsigned long could potentially invoke undefined behaviour because the size of an int is implementation dependent. The C++ standard specifies a 'minimum' size for an int, which is 2 bytes. This means that on a 16-bit machine an int is guaranteed to be 2 bytes, while on a 32-bit machine it could be either 2 or 4 bytes. The grading example needs at least 4 bytes to represent the data set of 30 students (one bit per student). Anything less would overflow the range of values an int could hold.

4.33.name: 4.33.md
4.33.text:
```text
someValue ? ++x, ++y : --x, --y
```

The intention of the expression is unclear. Perhaps it is to increment x and y, if someValue is true (i.e., 1) or decrement x and y, if someValue is false (i.e., 0). The problem, however, is that the conditional statement operator is higher in precedence than the comma operator, which means it will be evaluated first as such:

```cpp
(someValue ? ++x, ++y : --x), --y;
```

Note that the expression --y will always be evaluated after the conditional statement operator has been evaluated. This would lead to a surprising result if someValue is true.

To force the behaviour of the expression to confirm with the aforementioned intention, we must parenthesise the second comma operator's expression.

```cpp
someValue ? ++x, ++y : (--x, --y);
```

or better yet both:

```cpp
someValue ? (++x, ++y) : (--x, --y);
```
